title: Retina
content_html:
Retina

From Retinal Image to Reconstructed Recall

Light hits the retina, where it is transduced into neural signals. This raw sensory input is processed by the visual cortex in the occipital lobe. At this early stage, the image is closer to what you called a “photographic memory” — but only briefly, sensory memory or iconic memory lasts only milliseconds to a couple of seconds. To persist beyond seconds, the image must be encoded into short-term / working memory and then potentially consolidated into long-term memory.

Long-term storage is not photographic, it is distributed across networks, storing different features (shape, color, motion) in different cortical areas, and is linked to semantic memory (concepts and meanings), episodic memory (personal context), and emotional memory (amygdala tagging experiences with affect). When recalling, the brain reactivates patterns across these distributed networks. The recalled “image” is not the original sensory trace but a reconstruction influenced by semantics (knowledge and categories), logic (inferred structure e.g., remembering a square table as perfectly square even if it wasn’t), emotion (which can amplify, distort, or suppress details). Associations blend, merging details from similar events.

Some individuals report eidetic imagery (“photographic memory”), especially in children. But even then, these images are not perfect replications, they are still subject to reconstruction and interference.

So the flow looks like this:

Retina → sensory trace (fleeting) → distributed encoding (visual + semantic + emotional) → recall = reconstruction influenced by models of meaning, logic, and feeling.
